newsitem.title: USA: Rubin doesn't see U.S. contribution to Thai rescue.
newsitem.headline: Rubin doesn't see U.S. contribution to Thai rescue.

text.p: The United States backs a strong IMF loan program for Thailand, but does not expect to contribute its own money to any rescue package for the Asian nation, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Thursday.
"I don't expect we would be providing resources in a Mexico-type package," Rubin told Reuters in an interview.
The United States led the way in early 1995 in putting together an international rescue package for Mexico after the country came to the brink of defaulting on its foreign debt.

Rubin said that the International Monetary Fund should take the lead in helping Thailand and added that the United States had been working closely with both the IMF and Bangkok to help fashion an economic program for the Asian nation.

"We've been supportive of a strong IMF program that will both provide resources but also help the Thais institute the kinds of measures they need to be in a financially sound position," the Treasury chief said.
Earlier this week, Thailand began talking with the IMF about a loan program to help it weather a financial crisis brought on by a sharp drop in the value of its currency.
Japan has signalled its willingness to join in a rescue package for Thaialnd that could total up to $20 billion, provided it is backed by IMF-sanctioned economic reforms.
The fall-out from the Thai crisis has affected other countries in region, including the Philippines, which was also forced to devalue its currency and borrow from the IMF.
Rubin though doubted that Thailand's troubles posed the same sort of risks to the international financial system that Mexico's did in 1994/95.
"We have to watch and watch very carefully," he said. But, he added, "I don't think there are contagion risks anything like the magnitude you had with Mexico."
International investors are more sophisticated than they were back then and have learned to better distinguish one emerging market economy from the other, Rubin said.
The international community, including the IMF, is also better prepared, he added.
The IMF used fast-track regulations drawn up after the Mexico crisis to approve a $1.1 billion loan for the Philippines earlier this month.
Rubin praised Manila for moving quickly to deal with the financial fall-out from Thailand's currency crisis.
"I thought they handled themselves extremely well," he said.
